The compressor was designed under a NASA Research Announcement (NRA) contract with 2/3 NASA and 1/3 UTRC funding.
The design target was to increase efficiency at higher work factor while reducing the maximum diameter of the stage.
The impeller had a tip diameter of 6.5 inches, a rotational speed of 52,000 rpm, and a 30° backsweep.
The diffuser had a vaned topology with splitter vanes to improve performance.
The measured pressure ratio was 4.68 and the work factor was 0.81 at the design flow rate.
The measured polytropic efficiency was 85.5% and the stall margin was 7.5% at the design point.
The measured efficiency and stall margin were lower than pre-test CFD predictions by 2.4 and 4.5 percentage points, respectively.
Post-test CFD analysis identified unsteady impeller-diffuser interactions, flow-rate mismatch, and flow separation as the likely causes of the performance shortfall.
Recommendations included redesigning the diffuser and radial-to-axial bend to address the identified issues.
Lessons were learned about the importance of unsteady CFD simulations and turbulence model implementation for centrifugal compressors.
The impeller was successfully fabricated with runouts less than 2 mils and imbalance less than 0.5 oz-in.
The compressor was instrumented with steady-state and high-response pressure measurements to capture the flow physics.
A subsequent test with a vaneless diffuser was recommended to better isolate the impeller performance.
The design process readiness was established through validation of the CFD approach on a previous compressor design.
The final compressor design had a challenging reduction in radius ratio compared to conventional designs.
